name: Backfire Effect
description: Corrections aimed at debunking a false belief can, in some cases, strengthen commitment to the original belief instead of weakening it. In the current literature, the stronger claim that factual corrections usually backfire appears much shakier and more contingent than the label suggests.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to misinformation labels, trust-and-safety interventions, onboarding/error-correction copy, and AI explanation UX: teams often fear any correction will entrench the problem, but the evidence now suggests that worst-case intuition should be used carefully rather than assumed.
myth_risk_note: The 'worldview backfire effect' — that factual corrections on contested political/scientific topics paradoxically strengthen false beliefs — is not supported as a robust, generalizable phenomenon. Nyhan's original 2010 study found it in narrow subgroups; Wood & Porter's much larger 2018 direct replication found none across 52 issues, and a 2020 systematic review concludes it is not robust. This is a genuine 'zombie fact' — still widely cited in media and policy despite being substantially undercut by the largest direct test; even the original author has since walked back the general framing.
prevalence_note: Widely referenced in misinformation, fact-checking, trust-and-safety, and political-information design discussions because the dramatic 'corrections can make it worse' claim spread well beyond academia.

findings.description: Across five experiments, more than 10,100 subjects, and 52 potential backfire issues, Wood & Porter found no corrections capable of triggering factual backfire, concluding that the strong claim that factual corrections typically entrench false beliefs is far weaker and rarer than earlier work suggested.
findings.source_title: The Elusive Backfire Effect: Mass Attitudes’ Steadfast Factual Adherence

findings.description: Across four experiments using mock news articles with political misinformation and corrections, Nyhan & Reifler found that corrections often failed to reduce misperceptions among the target ideological group and in several cases appeared to backfire by increasing commitment to the original false claim.
findings.source_title: When Corrections Fail: The Persistence of Political Misperceptions

applications.title: Nyhan & Reifler's fake-newspaper-correction study: corrections that backfire
applications.description: In a 2006 study, political scientists Brendan Nyhan (University of Michigan) and Jason Reifler (Georgia State University) created fake newspaper articles about politically polarizing topics, each including a factual correction contradicting a widespread partisan misconception. Participants whose preexisting beliefs were most invested in the misconception often reported believing the original false claim even more strongly after reading the correction, rather than updating toward it.
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, peer-reviewed finding about why factual corrections can fail to change minds, not a persuasion or product-design technique. There is no manipulation dimension in the underlying research itself, though the finding has clear implications for anyone designing corrective UX content (error messages, fact-checks, in-product corrections).
